title: The Sour Book
blurb: A baker's lad lies hurt under a fallen shop sign, asking who Leonard Pask is, and the pad of pre-written dockets Ila uncovers has one name left to fill.

blocks.text: Six in the morning, and my bob is straight and still over the ironmonger's step.

Twelve days ago I stood behind the launderette glass across the road and watched Gervase Vosper kneel on this hollow step and tie Orla's snare, with a real fid, onto a real knot. Every morning since, before Dorrie's opens, I've come here and let my bob down on its silk, and every morning it has swung crooked towards the step and circled five times. Five strands. Serious weight. An old worn knot under a hundred years of feet, with something waiting on top of it that only I knew was there.
This morning the silk is a plumb line. The knot is gone. Somebody untied it before it was light.
A snare fires once, in the last minute of the dwell, on one named person, inside a mile.

Ten minutes ago Precious called down from the cab of the first 14 from Gullet Lane, the way she tells me everything, that there'd been an ambulance in Saltbox Lane at half five. A shop sign came down on a man walking to work.
Saltbox Lane is nine streets from this step.
I run.

Last night I did what the rulebook says anybody may do. I wrote a complaint in my best hand: a snare tied on the doorstep of the old ironmonger's, Hobday Street, by a knotter of the Bureau; five strands; recipient unknown; please swing it before anyone unties it. I didn't write his name. His name comes attached to Ferdie's, and I've given Ferdie my word.
I took it to the Registry night hatch on Tallow Row. Gwen, who sat across from me for two years and still gets a biscuit from me every Friday, read it twice and slid it back under the glass.
"Suspended clerks don't file, Ila. You know that." Then, more kindly: "And slack can't be shaped. It's on page one."

It is on page one. Page one is wrong. My own name rode an ambulance radio in March, on slack that Orla's snare had shaped. But I couldn't say that through a hatch, so I said thank you, Gwen, and went home, and told myself the rulebook would catch it in the morning.
I haven't told Orla. She told me she didn't ask who sold Ferdie his luck, and I can't tell her who tied her snare without telling her that.
For twelve evenings I walked the mile round that step, looking for whoever it was meant for. A mile round Hobday Street is tens of thousands of people, and I didn't know which one he wanted.
Now I do.

Saltbox Lane runs down to the old market, and it's already full of morning: crates, a sweeper's cart, a fish van backing up. Halfway down, a long painted board lies face down across the pavement in a spray of glass. Osgood and Daughter, Teas and Coffees, it said, when it was up. Its iron bracket has snapped clean off the wall. There's sawdust over a dark patch by the kerb, and a man in a council jacket is sweeping round it very carefully.
I take my bob out over the board. It circles once, wobbles, and goes quiet. Nothing here now. Whatever was coming has come.
A white van stands at the kerb with the cab door open and the radio going. The man unloading it wears a market apron and the face of somebody who hasn't been to bed.
"Were you here?" I ask him. "When it came down?"

"Saw it." He puts a crate on the pavement. "Lad in baker's whites, walking down to the ovens at the bottom, same as every morning. Twenty past five. The bracket went like a gunshot. I've parked under that sign eleven years."
"Is he alive?"
"Talking when they lifted him. His leg was..." He shows me with his hands, then stops. "He'll be a while."
"I'm Ila," I say. "What's your name?"
"Glyn." He looks at me properly. "You're not police."
"No. Glyn, did he hear anything? While he was lying there?"

Glyn rubs his face. "That's the bit I keep going back to. I'd the radio on, that phone-in they do for the night shifts. And the presenter says, 'Leonard Pask, you're on the air, go ahead, Leonard.' And the lad on the pavement, with his leg all wrong, lifts his head and says, 'Who's Leonard Pask?' Like that was the worst of it. He kept saying it. 'Who's Leonard Pask?' All the way into the ambulance."
The council man has stopped sweeping.

I know that name. I processed dockets in Registry for four years, and I know the Porters by their signatures the way Precious knows her regulars by their coats. Leonard Pask, Docket Porter, Cable Street. A big looping L and a small fierce k.
It isn't Vosper's name.
"Thank you, Glyn," I say. And to the council man: "What's yours?"
"Clive."
"Thank you, Clive."

I walk back up Saltbox Lane, and I don't run now. I did everything the rulebook says. I wrote it down and handed it in, and a man who walks to the ovens at twenty past five every morning is in hospital with his leg in pieces, asking the name of a stranger. The rulebook didn't catch anything. It was never going to.

The Amalgamated Society of Docket Porters keeps its hall on Cable Street, up a flight of brown stairs that smell of tea and wet coats. At seven the long room is full: Porters in donkey jackets waiting on the day's dockets, a chalkboard of jobs, an urn that ticks. Mags Danquah sits at a trestle table at the far end with a pile of paper and a pencil behind her ear. She sees me come in and doesn't get up.
"Management," she says. "At this hour."
"A man's been hurt on Saltbox Lane," I say. "A shop sign, at twenty past five. While he lay there, a radio said a name, and the name was Leonard Pask."
The talk at the nearest tables stops.
I've had the whole walk to be sure, and I am. I lay it out for her, plainly, the way she likes things.
"Item: the name rides. Item: it's the keeper's name. Item: so Leonard Pask did this."
Mags looks at me for a long moment. Then she turns in her chair.
"Lenny."
A man by the urn puts his cup down. He's sixty or so, thin, and he takes his cap off as he comes. His face is grey.
"Your book from last night," Mags says. "On the table."
"Mags, it was a clearance."
"On the table, Lenny."

He takes a fat little pad out of his inside pocket, bound in black card, the size of a paperback, and puts it in front of her. Docket tags, perforated down one edge, the kind Registry orders by the thousand. The top tag has been torn away. The stub it left behind repeats the job, the way every docket stub does: Field Allocation; clearance; doorstep, Hobday Street; five strands; triple rate. Keeper, L. Pask, in his big looping L.
And across the top of the stub, in pencil, in a slanting hand that isn't his, there's a man's name I don't know and a line under it. Saltbox Lane. On foot. Twenty past five.
Mags reads it. Then she turns the pad round so I can.
"He signed for a clearance," she says. "Not for a man under a sign. Somebody wrote the target."
I look at the pencil. I look at Lenny's signature, nowhere near it.
"I'm wrong," I say. "I'm wrong. The keeper isn't the one who aimed it."

"I never read the pencil," Lenny says. His voice is very small. "It's Mr Vosper's jobs. Triple rate. His man brings the book, you sign off the top at the untie, and nothing falls on you. Not a thing, Mags. Not so much as a stubbed toe. That's the beauty of it. I thought that was the beauty of it."
Nothing fell on him because there was nothing left to fall. All five strands went where the pencil said.
"Whose hand is the pencil?" I ask.

"Mr Vosper does the top lines himself. Says it saves us the bother." Lenny swallows. "The book goes round. Whoever did the last job keeps it till the next. His man calls it the sour book. I thought that was a joke about the paper."
The card has gone yellow at the edges. It isn't a joke about the paper. A sour is what you call slack that has been shaped into bad luck, aimed at someone, and sold.
Mags lays her palm flat on the table, on top of the book.
"No member," she says, not loudly, to the whole room, "shall put his hand to any paper the whole of which has not first been read to him. That's the rule, Lenny. It was the rule in your dad's time."
"I know, Mags."
"Sit down. Have your tea. You'll sign nothing of Mr Vosper's again."

She doesn't stop me when I reach for the book. I turn back through the stubs, one at a time. Each one has a Porter's name at the bottom and Vosper's pencil at the top. Then, in the middle of March, three in a row.
J. Mallender. Quay Street, a cyclist. K. Farrow. A yard, a ladder. D. Abara. The fish quay, a pallet.
Mags sees them the same moment I do. Her hand on the black card doesn't move.
"Joyce wouldn't have known," Lenny says from his chair. "You don't read the pencil."

I shut my eyes, and Dad's lock-up wall is there, chalk and all. The thin clusters. Down by the docks. Round the old market. Up by the bridges. Complaints that Registry stamped No Action, because nobody could find a knot at those addresses when they went to look.
"They're his," I say. "Mags, the complaints in my drawer. The places where nobody found anything. They're his customers, and the people his customers wanted hurt."
Mags looks at me across the trestle the way she looked at me in Dorrie's in March, as if I'm a Bureau building she'd quite like to see come down. Then something in her face changes its mind.
"Right," she says. "Management or not. You'd better sit."
I sit. Somebody puts a mug of tea by my elbow, and I ask his name, and it's Bevan, and I thank him.
"I want to take this to Standards," I say.

"And they'll lose it in a drawer." Mags's palm comes down on the black card again, flat. "I've read your schedule, love. I know what the Bureau does with paper it doesn't like. Members' paper stays in the hall."

My phone buzzes in my pocket. A Standards number. A woman's voice, polite and bored: my suspension review will be heard at two o'clock this afternoon on Tallow Row, and I'm to wait in the lobby until called.
"Go on, then," Mags says. "Go and be reviewed."
"Will you read it all? Right to the back?"
"I'll read what the membership needs read."
I'm in the Bureau lobby at twenty to two, because I am always early, and Stan at the front desk gives me the look you give a parcel that has come back marked return to sender.
"Afternoon, Ila. They've not found you a chair, I'm afraid."
"That's all right, Stan. How's your knee?"
"Rotten. Thanks for asking."
So I stand, and because I'm standing next to it, I read the founding docket.

I've walked past it every working day for four years. It's in a glass case by the Standards door: an old card tag gone the colour of strong tea, its string cut short and pinned flat on green baize. Everyone at the Bureau knows what it is the way you know what a war memorial is. You'd never stop to read it. I read it now. The ink is brown and very upright, and on the keeper's line there's no name.
It says: the Sexton for the time being.
"Stan," I say, "how does an office sign anything? An office hasn't got a hand."
"Couldn't tell you, love. It's been there longer than the carpet."

Under the signature there's a round blot of old red wax, cracked at one edge. Pressed into it, side by side, are five small marks, each a different shape. One is a neat square. One is like a little star. One is hardly more than a notch. I've cleaned enough fid points in Registry to know a tool end when I see one. These were made by the points of five different fids.
The brass label underneath says: Founding docket. Seal impressions.
I bend closer, until my breath mists the glass.
"Clerk Brandt."
I straighten so fast I nearly knock my head on the case.

The Sexton of the Bureau of Causal Repair is a small woman in grey, with her hair pinned flat and her hands folded in front of her, and she is standing beside me as if she has been there a while. I've only ever seen her from the far end of the lobby, at the foot of the tower stair, at five to nine. Sexton Honoria Tregear. Up close she is softer than I expected, and exact, the way a ruler is exact.
"Thank you for your patience, Clerk Brandt," she says. "I know these reviews are tiresome."
"Not at all, Sexton." And then, because the question is still in my mouth and I can't help it: "Sexton, how does an office sign anything?"
She looks at the case, not at me. For a moment I think she is going to answer.
"Tell me," she says instead, in the same soft voice. "Are the Nettlecombe Allotments still so very loud?"
Everything in me goes as still as my bob this morning.
I have never once said the word Nettlecombe inside this building.
"I..." I say.
"Your review is deferred," says the Sexton. "Standards will write to you. Thank you. That will be all."
She walks away to the tower stair, and her heels on the old tiles keep perfect time, and the door closes behind her without a sound. Stan has found something very interesting to read on his desk.
She didn't answer my question. She answered one I hadn't asked. She knows where I go in the afternoons, and she wants me to know she knows.

Mags is at my window table in Dorrie's when I come out, with a pot of tea for two and the black book squared up in front of her. She found me here once before, in March, to tell me what she thought of Management. She hasn't come to do that today.
"Deferred," I tell her.

"Deferred is what they say instead of no." She pushes the book across. "I've a branch meeting at five, and I'll not stand up in front of the membership with this half read. You've your drawer in your head, love. Go through it. Tell me which of these is which."

So I go through it, stub by stub, and she stands behind my chair and reads over my shoulder. I give her each address and the complaint that came from it, and who complained, and when. The docks. The old market. The bridges. Every pencil line in Vosper's slanting hand lands on a place I know. It takes nearly an hour. Dorrie brings more hot water without being asked, and I thank her.
After the stubs come the tags nobody has torn off yet. A dozen of them, blank, the card still clean.
Then, at the very back, one more.
It's been filled in, but only partly. The job line is empty. There's no site, no date and no strands, and the keeper's line at the bottom is waiting for a signature that isn't there.
Only the pencil across the top has been written, in the same slanting hand as all the others.
Behind me, Mags stops breathing.
The target line reads Mags Danquah.
